grammar.title: Past simple vs past continuous
grammar.summary: Use the past simple for finished actions and events in the past, often one after another. Use the past continuous for an action that was in progress at a moment in the past, or for the background of a story. A short action often interrupts a longer one.
grammar.summaryMn: Past simple-ийг өнгөрсөнд болж дууссан үйл, дараалан болсон үйл явдалд хэрэглэнэ. Past continuous-ийг өнгөрсөн тодорхой мөчид үргэлжилж байсан үйл болон түүхийн арын дэвсгэрт хэрэглэнэ. Богино үйл ихэвчлэн урт, үргэлжилж буй үйлийг тасалдуулдаг.
structure: Past simple: I/you/he/she/we/they worked · went (irregular) · Did you work? · She didn't work.
Past continuous: was/were + verb-ing · I was working · They were talking · Were you working? · He wasn't listening.
Interrupted action: past continuous + when + past simple → I was walking home when I saw her.
Two long actions at the same time: while + past continuous → While I was cooking, he was watching TV.

usage.use: Finished actions and events in the past
usage.example: We met in 2015 and got married two years later.

usage.use: A series of actions, one after another
usage.example: He stood up, walked to the door and left.

usage.use: An action in progress at a particular time in the past
usage.example: At eight o'clock last night I was having dinner with my parents.
usage.useMn: Өнгөрсөн тодорхой цагт үргэлжилж байсан үйл

usage.use: A longer action interrupted by a shorter one
usage.example: I was waiting for the bus when I bumped into my old teacher.

usage.use: Background description at the start of a story
usage.example: It was snowing and people were hurrying home.

examples.en: I was living in Darkhan when I met my wife.
examples.note: Background situation (past continuous) + the main event (past simple).

examples.en: While we were talking, my phone rang three times.
examples.note: 'While' usually goes with the longer action.

examples.en: When the teacher came in, the students stopped talking.
examples.note: Past simple + past simple: first the teacher came in, then they stopped.

examples.en: What were you doing at ten o'clock last night?
examples.note: A question about an action in progress at a past time.

contrast.with: Past simple vs past continuous after 'when'

pairs.a: When she arrived, we had dinner.
pairs.b: When she arrived, we were having dinner.
pairs.why: In the first sentence, dinner started after she arrived. In the second, dinner was already in progress when she arrived.
pairs.whyMn: Эхнийхэд тэр ирсний дараа бид хоол идэж эхэлсэн. Хоёр дахьд нь түүнийг ирэхэд бид аль хэдийн хоол идэж байсан.

pairs.a: I read a book last night.
pairs.b: I was reading a book at midnight.
pairs.why: The first is a complete action. The second shows the action was in progress at one moment.
pairs.whyMn: Эхнийх нь бүрэн дууссан үйл, хоёр дахь нь тодорхой мөчид үргэлжилж байсан үйл.

mistakes.wrong: I was meeting my husband in 2010.
mistakes.why: Meeting someone for the first time is a short, complete event, so use the past simple.
mistakes.whyMn: Анх танилцах нь богино, дууссан үйл явдал тул past simple хэрэглэнэ.

mistakes.wrong: When I was walking home, I was seeing an accident.
mistakes.right: When I was walking home, I saw an accident.
mistakes.why: The short action that interrupts uses the past simple. 'See' is also a state verb and is rarely continuous.
mistakes.whyMn: Тасалдуулж буй богино үйл past simple байна. 'See' нь байдал илэрхийлэх үйл үг тул -ing хэлбэр бараг авдаггүй.

mistakes.why: Use 'were' with you, we and they.

mistakes.wrong: Did you sleeping when I called?
mistakes.right: Were you sleeping when I called?
mistakes.why: Past continuous questions use was/were, not did.
mistakes.whyMn: Past continuous-ийн асуултад did биш was/were хэрэглэнэ.

guided.prompt: I ___ TV when the lights went out.
guided.explanation: A longer action (watching TV) was interrupted by a short one (the lights went out).

guided.prompt: Yesterday I got up, ___ a shower and went to work.
guided.explanation: A series of finished actions, one after another → past simple.

guided.prompt: While my parents ___ in the garden, somebody knocked on the door.
guided.explanation: 'While' + the longer action; 'parents' is plural → were working.

guided.prompt: ___ you driving when the police stopped you?
guided.explanation: Past continuous question with 'you' → Were you + -ing.

guided.prompt: Which sentence means the phone call interrupted the meal?
options: When he called, we had lunch.
When he called, we were having lunch.
guided.explanation: The past continuous shows lunch was already in progress.

free.prompt: I ___ (walk) through the park when I bumped into my old classmate.
free.explanation: The longer, interrupted action → was + walking.
An action in progress at a past time → were you + doing.

free.prompt: They ___ (not / listen) when the teacher explained the homework.

free.sentence: When I was a student, I was meeting my best friend at a concert.
answers: When I was a student, I met my best friend at a concert.
free.explanation: Meeting someone for the first time is a single event → past simple.

free.prompt: Join the two sentences into one. Use the word given.
free.sentence: She was cooking. Her friend called.
answers: She was cooking when her friend called.
When her friend called, she was cooking.
free.explanation: Longer action (past continuous) + when + shorter action (past simple).

grammar.title: used to / didn't use to
grammar.summary: Use 'used to' + base verb for past habits and past states that are not true now. It shows that something has changed.
grammar.summaryMn: 'Used to' + үйл үгийн анхны хэлбэрийг өнгөрсөнд давтагддаг байсан ч одоо болисон зуршил, одоо үнэн биш болсон байдлыг илэрхийлэхэд хэрэглэнэ. Энэ нь ямар нэг зүйл өөрчлөгдсөнийг харуулна.
structure: Positive: subject + used to + base verb · I used to live in Erdenet.
Negative: subject + didn't use to + base verb · She didn't use to like coffee.
Question: Did + subject + use to + base verb? · Did you use to play football?
Another negative: never used to · He never used to call me.

usage.use: Past habits (repeated actions) that have stopped
usage.example: My grandfather used to ride a horse to school.
usage.useMn: Өнгөрсөнд давтагддаг байсан, одоо болисон зуршил

usage.use: Past states that are not true now
usage.example: There used to be a cinema on this street.
We used to be close, but now we rarely talk.

usage.use: Not for single events or an exact number of times: use the past simple
usage.example: I went to Japan in 2019. (not 'I used to go')
usage.useMn: Нэг удаагийн үйлд used to хэрэглэхгүй, past simple хэрэглэнэ

examples.en: I used to be very shy, but now I'm quite confident.
examples.note: A past state that has changed.

examples.en: We didn't use to have a car when I was a child.
Did you use to fight with your brother?
My parents used to live in the countryside. They moved to the city in 1998.
examples.note: 'Used to' for the long situation; past simple for the single event.

pairs.a: I used to play basketball every weekend.
pairs.why: 'Used to' describes a repeated past habit. The past simple describes one event.
pairs.whyMn: 'Used to' давтагддаг байсан зуршил, past simple нэг удаагийн үйл явдлыг илэрхийлнэ.

pairs.a: She used to live in Khovd.
pairs.b: She lived in Khovd for three years.
pairs.why: With an exact length of time ('for three years'), we normally use the past simple.
pairs.whyMn: Тодорхой хугацаа ('for three years') заасан бол ихэвчлэн past simple хэрэглэнэ.

mistakes.wrong: I use to play football when I was a child.
mistakes.right: I used to play football when I was a child.
mistakes.why: In positive sentences, write 'used to' with -d.

mistakes.wrong: Did you used to live here?
mistakes.right: Did you use to live here?

mistakes.wrong: I used to go to Paris last year.
mistakes.right: I went to Paris last year.
mistakes.why: 'Used to' is for repeated habits or long states, not for one event.
mistakes.whyMn: Нэг удаагийн үйлд used to хэрэглэхгүй.

mistakes.wrong: I used to getting up early.
mistakes.right: I used to get up early.
mistakes.why: 'Used to' is followed by the base verb. ('I'm used to getting up early' means something different: I am familiar with it.)
mistakes.whyMn: 'Used to'-ийн дараа үйл үгийн анхны хэлбэр орно. 'I'm used to getting up early' гэвэл 'эрт босоход дассан' гэсэн өөр утгатай.

guided.prompt: When I was a child, I ___ milk. Now I love it.
guided.explanation: A past state that has changed → used to + base verb.

options: There use to be a park here.
There used to be a park here.
There was used to be a park here.

guided.prompt: ___ you use to walk to school?

options: My dad used to smoke, but he stopped years ago.
We used to go to the lake every summer.
I used to lose my phone last Tuesday.
guided.explanation: 'Last Tuesday' is one event → I lost my phone last Tuesday.

free.prompt: My brother ___ (be) very shy, but now he's a TV presenter.
free.explanation: A past state that is not true now.

free.prompt: I ___ (not / like) vegetables when I was young.
free.explanation: Negative: didn't + use to + base verb.

free.sentence: Did your parents used to be strict?
answers: Did your parents use to be strict?

free.prompt: Rewrite the sentence with 'used to'. Use the word given.
free.sentence: When I was a student, I often stayed up all night. I don't now.
answers: When I was a student, I used to stay up all night.
I used to stay up all night when I was a student.
free.explanation: A past habit that has stopped → used to + stay.

pronunciation.title: Weak forms: was /wəz/ and were /wə/
pronunciation.explanation: In natural speech, 'was' and 'were' are usually not stressed in the middle of a sentence. 'Was' sounds like /wəz/ and 'were' like /wə/: short and quiet, with the schwa sound /ə/. We use the strong forms /wɒz/ and /wɜː/ only at the end of a sentence, in short answers or for emphasis. Negative forms (wasn't, weren't) are always strong. 'Used to' is also linked in speech: /ˈjuːstə/.
pronunciation.explanationMn: Ярианд 'was', 'were' өгүүлбэрийн дунд ихэвчлэн өргөлтгүй, богино дуудагдана: was — /wəz/, were — /wə/ (сул /ə/ эгшигтэй). Өгүүлбэрийн төгсгөлд, богино хариултад эсвэл онцлох үед хүчтэй хэлбэр /wɒz/, /wɜː/ хэрэглэнэ. Үгүйсгэх хэлбэр (wasn't, weren't) үргэлж хүчтэй дуудагдана. 'Used to'-г /ˈjuːstə/ гэж холбож хэлнэ.

items.tip: At the end of a sentence, 'was' is strong.
Short answers use the strong form.

shadowing.text: I was waiting for the bus when I saw her.
shadowing.stress: I was WAITing for the BUS when I SAW her.

shadowing.text: What were you doing when he called?
shadowing.stress: WHAT were you DOing when he CALLED?
shadowing.tip: 'were you' is quick and light: wuh-yuh.

shadowing.text: We were talking about it, but she wasn't listening.
shadowing.stress: We were TALKing aBOUT it, but she WASn't LIStening.

shadowing.text: We used to be really close.
shadowing.stress: We USED to be REALly CLOSE.

spokenForms.note: Weak form in the middle of a sentence: I was /wəz/ working.
Weak form before a verb-ing: they were /wə/ talking.
In this meaning it always has /s/, never /z/.

lessons.title: Firstborn, middle or youngest?
objectives: Understand the main idea and details of a magazine article about birth order
Describe the personalities of people in your family

warmup.intro: Think about your family. Are you the oldest child, a middle child, the youngest or an only child?

questions.prompt: Which word describes a person who always does what they promise?
The article in this lesson is called 'Does Birth Order Shape Who We Are?' What do you think it is about?
options: How to choose a name for a baby
Whether your position in the family affects your personality
How to be a good parent
questions.explanation: 'Birth order' means whether you were born first, second, last and so on.

vocabulary.definition: able to be trusted to do what you promise
examples: Tuya is really reliable — if she says she'll help, she always does.
I need a reliable person to look after my dog while I'm away.
vocabulary.mistake: The stress is on the second syllable: re-LI-able, not RE-li-able.

vocabulary.definition: relaxed and not easily worried or annoyed
examples: My dad is very easy-going — nothing makes him angry.
She's an easy-going person, so she's easy to live with.
vocabulary.note: Always positive. 'Laid-back' is an informal synonym.

vocabulary.definition: happy to give money, time or help to other people
examples: My grandmother is very generous — she always gives us money on our birthdays.
It was generous of you to pay for lunch.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'It's generous of you', not 'It's generous for you'.

vocabulary.definition: thinking only about yourself and not about other people
examples: It was selfish of him to eat all the cake.
Don't be so selfish — let your sister use the computer too.

vocabulary.definition: not willing to change your ideas or opinions, even when you should
examples: My brother is so stubborn — he never admits he's wrong.
She was too stubborn to ask for help.
vocabulary.note: Usually negative, but it can sound positive when it means 'determined'.

vocabulary.definition: friendly and happy to meet and talk to new people
examples: Our youngest son is very outgoing and makes friends everywhere.
You need to be outgoing to work in sales.
vocabulary.note: For things, 'outgoing' means 'leaving': outgoing calls, the outgoing president.

vocabulary.definition: able to make good, practical decisions
examples: My older sister was always the sensible one in our family.
Wearing a warm hat in January is a sensible idea.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Sensible' is not 'sensitive'. A sensible person makes good decisions; a sensitive person has strong feelings.

vocabulary.definition: easily upset by what people say or do; also good at understanding other people's feelings
examples: Be careful what you say — he's very sensitive about his weight.
She's a sensitive listener and always knows when something is wrong.
vocabulary.mistake: Use 'sensitive about' a topic: 'sensitive about his age', not 'sensitive for his age'.

vocabulary.definition: always telling other people what to do
examples: My big sister was really bossy when we were kids.
Stop being so bossy — I can decide for myself.
vocabulary.note: Informal and negative. A person who organises others well at work is 'a good leader', not 'bossy'.

vocabulary.definition: sure of yourself and your abilities
examples: After a few months in the job, she felt much more confident.
He's confident about speaking in public.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'confident about something', not 'confident for something'.

vocabulary.definition: always supporting a friend, family member or group, even in difficult times
examples: Dogs are famous for being loyal to their owners.
She stayed loyal to her friend when everyone else was criticising him.

reading.title: Does Birth Order Shape Who We Are?
text: Think about your family. Are you the oldest child, a middle child, the youngest or an only child? For more than a hundred years, psychologists have asked whether our position in the family shapes our personality. Many people are sure that it does.

According to the popular theory, firstborn children are often sensible and reliable. When they were young, their parents gave them a lot of responsibility, and they often looked after their younger brothers and sisters. The downside is that some of them become a little bossy. Middle children, on the other hand, are said to be easy-going and good at finding solutions, because they grew up between two strong personalities.

The youngest child is often described as outgoing and confident: the funny one who loves attention. Some people say the youngest can also be a little selfish, because everyone always looked after them. In Mongolia, the youngest son traditionally stays with his parents and takes care of the family home, so he is often expected to be especially loyal to the family.
Only children have a reputation too. People sometimes think they are stubborn or too sensitive, but many only children say they learned to be independent and generous with their time.

So is the theory true? Recent large studies suggest that the effect is very small. When researchers compared thousands of brothers and sisters, they found almost no difference in personality. Our character depends much more on our genes, our friends and our experiences. Perhaps we believe in birth order because it is an easy way to explain why our brother is so different from us — and it gives families something to argue about at dinner.

glossary.meaning: a scientist who studies the mind and behaviour
the first child born in a family
a duty to take care of something or someone
the parts of your body cells that come from your parents and control how you develop

questions.prompt: What is the main idea of the article?
options: Firstborn children are more successful than their brothers and sisters.
There is a popular theory about birth order and personality, but research shows the effect is small.
Parents should treat all their children in the same way.
Only children have the most difficult personalities.
questions.explanation: The article describes the popular theory and then says large studies found very little effect.

questions.prompt: According to the popular theory, firstborn children often looked after their younger brothers and sisters.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2: 'they often looked after their younger brothers and sisters.'

questions.prompt: According to the popular theory, middle children love being the centre of attention.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: it is the youngest child who 'loves attention'.

questions.prompt: Only children usually earn more money than people with brothers and sisters.
Match each type of child with the personality the popular theory gives them.
pairs: sensible and reliable, but sometimes bossy
easy-going and good at finding solutions
outgoing and confident, but sometimes selfish
independent, but sometimes seen as stubborn

questions.prompt: In Mongolia, who traditionally stays with the parents and takes care of the family home?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: 'the youngest son traditionally stays with his parents'.

questions.prompt: In paragraph 4, 'reputation' means…
options: what people generally think about someone

questions.prompt: Why does the writer think people still believe in birth order?
options: Because parents want their children to be different.
Because it is part of Mongolian tradition.
Because it is a simple way to explain differences between brothers and sisters.
questions.explanation: Last paragraph: 'it is an easy way to explain why our brother is so different from us'.

quiz.prompt: My sister never lends anyone anything. She's so ___.
Which word is the OPPOSITE of 'outgoing'?
'He's very sensible' means he…
options: always tells people what to do

quiz.prompt: Match the adjectives with the descriptions.
pairs: always tells others what to do
never changes his or her mind

quiz.prompt: It was very ___ of you to pay for everyone's dinner.
Be careful — Dorj is very ___ about his exam results, so don't mention them.

lessons.title: How did you two meet?
objectives: Choose correctly between the past simple and the past continuous
Use when and while to connect the actions in a story
Tell the story of how you met someone important

warmup.intro: Every couple and every friendship has a 'how we met' story. First, a quick grammar check.

questions.prompt: I ___ my best friend at university in 2012.
questions.explanation: Meeting someone is a single finished event → past simple.

questions.prompt: What ___ you doing at eight o'clock last night?
questions.explanation: An action in progress at a past time → were you doing.

vocabulary.definition: to meet someone you know by chance
examples: I bumped into my old English teacher at the supermarket yesterday.
You'll never guess who I bumped into on the bus!
vocabulary.note: Informal. It can also mean to hit something by accident: 'I bumped into the door.'

vocabulary.definition: the opinion you form when you meet someone or see something for the first time
examples: My first impression of him was that he was a bit arrogant.
You only get one chance to make a good first impression.
vocabulary.mistake: We 'make' an impression, not 'do' or 'give' an impression.

vocabulary.definition: to start to love someone romantically
examples: They fell in love while they were working at the same hotel.
I fell in love with the city the first time I visited.
collocations: fall in love at first sight
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'fall in love with someone', not 'fall in love to someone'. Irregular: fall – fell – fallen.

vocabulary.definition: to have a romantic relationship with someone
examples: They went out for two years before they got engaged.
Is your brother going out with anyone at the moment?
vocabulary.note: Informal. 'Go out' also means leaving home for fun ('Let's go out tonight'); the context shows the meaning.

vocabulary.definition: to ask someone to marry you
examples: He proposed to her on Zaisan Hill at sunset.
She was so surprised when he proposed that she started crying.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'He proposed to her', not 'He proposed her'.
vocabulary.note: In formal English it also means 'suggest': 'I propose a short break.'

vocabulary.definition: having agreed to marry someone
examples: We got engaged last summer, and the wedding is in June.
Did you know that Bold and Saraa are engaged?
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'engaged to someone', not 'engaged with someone'.
vocabulary.note: In British English a phone line can also be 'engaged' (busy).

vocabulary.definition: to become husband and wife
examples: My parents got married in 1995.
They're getting married in a traditional ceremony next month.
collocations: get married in (a place / a year)
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'She got married to a doctor' or 'She married a doctor', not 'She married with a doctor'.

vocabulary.definition: a day when you remember something important that happened on the same date in an earlier year
examples: Tomorrow is my parents' 30th wedding anniversary.
We went to a nice restaurant to celebrate our first anniversary.
vocabulary.mistake: An anniversary is not a birthday. Use 'birthday' for the day a person was born.

vocabulary.definition: to end a romantic relationship
examples: They broke up after five years together.
She broke up with her boyfriend because he was always late.
vocabulary.note: The noun is 'a break-up'. For married couples, people usually say 'separate' or 'get divorced'.

speaking.prompt: Tell the story of how you met someone important in your life — a partner, a best friend or a colleague. Where were you? What were you doing? What happened next?
speaking.promptMn: Амьдралд тань чухал нэгэн хүн — хань, дотны найз эсвэл хамт ажилладаг хүнтэйгээ хэрхэн танилцсан түүхээ ярь. Та хаана байсан бэ? Юу хийж байсан бэ? Дараа нь юу болсон бэ?
points: Set the scene: when and where it was and what was happening (past continuous)
The moment you met (past simple)
Your first impression of the person
What happened after that
speaking.sample: I met my wife about ten years ago. I was working in a small bookshop in the centre of Ulaanbaatar, and she was looking for a present for her father. It was snowing outside and the shop was very quiet. She asked me to recommend a history book, and we started talking. My first impression was that she was a bit serious, but then she laughed at one of my jokes. A week later, I bumped into her again at a café near the shop. We went out for two years, and then I proposed on her birthday. We got married in 2017.

quiz.prompt: I ___ a shower when the doorbell rang.
While we ___ (walk) along the river, he proposed.
They met in 2010, ___ in 2012 and got married in 2014.
quiz.explanation: A series of single events → past simple.

quiz.prompt: Tap the part with the mistake.
quiz.explanation: 'Everybody' takes a singular verb → was dancing.

lessons.title: Falling out and making up
objectives: Understand a conversation about a problem between two friends
Use words and phrases for arguments and making up
Pronounce the weak forms of was and were
Give your opinion on what makes a good friend

warmup.intro: Have you ever had an argument with a good friend? How did it end?

questions.prompt: If two friends 'fall out', they…
options: meet again after a long time
have an argument and stop being friendly

vocabulary.definition: having a strong friendship or relationship
examples: Nara and I have been close since primary school.
I'm very close to my grandmother.
vocabulary.mistake: The adjective ends in /s/: /kləʊs/. The verb 'close the door' ends in /z/: /kləʊz/.

vocabulary.definition: to argue with someone and stop being friendly
examples: I fell out with my cousin over some money.
They fell out years ago and still don't speak to each other.
vocabulary.note: British English, informal. The noun is 'a falling-out'.

vocabulary.definition: to become friends again after an argument
examples: They had a big argument but made up the next day.
Have you made up with your sister yet?
vocabulary.note: 'Make up' has other meanings too: to invent (make up a story) and the noun 'make-up' (cosmetics).

vocabulary.definition: an angry disagreement between people
examples: We had an argument about who should pay for the tickets.
I hate arguments, so I usually stay quiet.
vocabulary.mistake: Spelling: 'argument', not 'arguement'. We 'have' an argument, not 'do' or 'make' one.

vocabulary.definition: to say that you are sorry for something you did
examples: I apologised to her for forgetting her birthday.
He never apologises, even when he's wrong.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'apologise to someone for something', not 'apologise someone'.

vocabulary.definition: to believe that someone is honest and will not hurt you; the feeling that you can believe someone
examples: I trust her completely — she would never lie to me.
After he read my messages, I lost my trust in him.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'I trust you', not 'I trust to you'.

vocabulary.definition: unhappy because someone has something you want, or because you think someone you love likes another person
examples: He gets jealous when his girlfriend talks to other men.
I was a bit jealous of my sister's new job.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'jealous of someone', not 'jealous on' or 'jealous to someone'.

vocabulary.definition: shared by two or more people (interests, opinions or experiences)
examples: We have a lot in common — we both love hiking and old films.
My brother and I have nothing in common.
collocations: have something in common with someone
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'We have a lot in common', not 'We have a lot of common'.

vocabulary.definition: unhappy or worried because something bad has happened
examples: She was really upset when she heard the news.
Don't get upset — I was only joking.
vocabulary.mistake: The stress is on the second syllable: up-SET. Say 'upset about something', not 'upset for something'.

listening.title: I think I've lost my best friend
listening.context: Emma tells her colleague Dan about an argument with her best friend, Lucy.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: You look a bit down, Emma. Is everything OK?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: Not really. I had a big argument with Lucy on Saturday, and we haven't spoken since.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: Lucy? But you two are so close. What happened?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: Well, we were having lunch in town, and I was telling her about my new job. While I was talking, she was looking at her phone the whole time.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: Oh, that's annoying.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: I know! So I said, 'You never listen to me.' And she got really upset and left.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: Hmm. Maybe she was worried about something?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: That's the thing. Her sister sent me a message last night. Lucy's mum was in hospital on Saturday, and Lucy was waiting for news from the doctors.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: Oh no. So it was just a misunderstanding.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: Exactly. And now I feel terrible. I used to think I was a good friend.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: You are a good friend. You just didn't know. Why don't you call her and apologise?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: I'm worried she won't answer. She can be a bit stubborn.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: Then send her a message first. Say you're sorry and ask about her mum. Friends fall out all the time. The important thing is that you make up.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.text: You're right. I'll text her now. Thanks, Dan.

speaking.sample: In my opinion, a good friend is someone you can trust completely. The most important thing is honesty, but a good friend also needs to be loyal and patient. For example, a few years ago I fell out with my closest friend, Anu. We were planning a trip together, and I forgot to book the train tickets. She was really upset, and we didn't speak for a month. In the end I apologised, and we made up. Now we're even closer than before. That's why I think real friends can have arguments — the important thing is that they talk about the problem.

warmup.intro: Think about an older person you admired when you were a child — a parent, a grandparent, a teacher or a coach.

vocabulary.definition: to change from a child into an adult; to spend your childhood somewhere
examples: I grew up in a small town in Arkhangai.
What did you want to be when you grew up?
vocabulary.mistake: Don't say 'I was grown up in Darkhan'. Say 'I grew up in Darkhan'.

vocabulary.definition: to look after a child until he or she is an adult
examples: My grandparents brought me up because my parents worked in another city.
It isn't easy to bring up three children alone.
vocabulary.mistake: Parents bring up children; children grow up. Don't say 'My parents grew me up'.
vocabulary.note: It can also mean 'start talking about a subject': 'Don't bring up politics at dinner.'

vocabulary.definition: to look or behave like an older member of your family
vocabulary.mn: (эцэг эх, өвөг дээдэстээ) адилхан байх, төстэй байх
examples: I take after my father — we're both stubborn.
She really takes after her grandmother: she's calm and generous.
vocabulary.mistake: Use it only for family members, and not in the continuous: 'She takes after her mum', not 'She is taking after her mum'.

vocabulary.definition: to admire and respect someone
examples: I always looked up to my older cousin — he was clever and kind.
Young players look up to him because he works so hard.

vocabulary.definition: a member of your family
examples: During Tsagaan Sar we visit all our relatives.
Most of my relatives live in the countryside.
vocabulary.note: A 'close relative' is a parent, child, brother or sister; a 'distant relative' is, for example, a second cousin.

vocabulary.definition: a brother or sister
examples: Do you have any siblings?
I'm the oldest of four siblings.
vocabulary.note: A little formal. In conversation people often ask, 'Have you got any brothers or sisters?'

vocabulary.definition: expecting people to obey rules completely
examples: My father used to be very strict about homework.
Our teacher was strict, but she was fair.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'strict with children' and 'strict about homework', not 'strict to children'.

vocabulary.definition: all the people of about the same age; one level of a family (grandparents, parents, children)
examples: Three generations of my family live in the same house.
My parents' generation didn't use to have mobile phones.

vocabulary.definition: to stop working, usually because you have reached a certain age
examples: My grandfather retired when he was sixty and started keeping bees.
She wants to retire early and travel.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'He retired' or 'He is retired', not 'He went to pension' (a direct translation).

phrases.whenToUse: Telling a story about meeting a friend or partner. Natural in speech and informal writing, not in formal reports.
phrases.example: We met at a friend's party and hit it off straight away.

phrases.phrase: She's the kind of person who…
phrases.meaning: used to describe someone's typical behaviour
phrases.whenToUse: Describing someone's personality, in speech or writing. Very useful in descriptions and emails.
phrases.example: My aunt is the kind of person who always remembers your birthday.

phrases.meaning: quite a … (used before a noun, often to make a criticism softer)
phrases.whenToUse: In conversation, to soften a negative description. Avoid it in formal writing.
phrases.example: My brother is a bit of a perfectionist.

phrases.meaning: used to introduce a strong memory
phrases.whenToUse: Starting a story about a memory, in speech or informal writing.
phrases.example: I'll never forget the time my grandfather taught me to ride a horse.

phrases.meaning: when I think about it now
phrases.whenToUse: Giving your opinion now about something in the past. Works in speech, emails and descriptions.
phrases.example: Looking back, I think my parents were right to be strict.

phrases.phrase: We go back a long way.
phrases.meaning: We have known each other for many years.
phrases.whenToUse: Talking about old friends in conversation.
phrases.example: Bat and I go back a long way — we were at school together.

writing.prompt: Write a description of a person who was important to you when you were a child (for example, a grandparent, a teacher or an older cousin). Say who they were, what they were like, what you used to do together and why they were important to you.
writing.promptMn: Бага байхад тань чухал байсан хүний (жишээ нь өвөө эмээ, багш, ах эгч) тухай тайлбар бичээрэй. Тэр хэн байсан, ямар зантай байсан, та хоёр хамт юу хийдэг байсан, яагаад танд чухал байсныг бичээрэй.
points: Who the person was and how you knew them

One special memory (past simple and past continuous)
Why they were important — looking back
phrases: He/She was the kind of person who…
writing.sample:
When I was a child, the person I looked up to most was my grandfather. He brought me up for a few years because my parents were working in Erdenet. He was a retired teacher, and he was strict but very generous. He was the kind of person who never shouted, even when I broke things.

Every summer we used to stay in the countryside. We used to get up early, milk the cows and ride horses together. I'll never forget the time he taught me to play chess. It was raining, and we were sitting in the ger and drinking milk tea.

Looking back, I think I take after him — I'm patient, and I love chess too.

reading.title: The Friend I Found Again
text: When I was ten, my best friend was a girl called Sara. We lived on the same street in Zuunkharaa, and we used to do everything together. We walked to school together, did our homework at her kitchen table and spent every summer by the river. People used to call us 'the twins', although we didn't look alike at all.

Then, when we were thirteen, Sara's father got a job in Ulaanbaatar and the family moved away. We promised to write to each other every week. For a few months we did, but then the letters stopped. I was busy with my new school, and I suppose she was too. Slowly, we lost contact.

Twenty years later, I was scrolling through social media one evening when I saw a familiar face. It was a photo of a woman at a school reunion, and she was smiling exactly like Sara used to. I sent her a message, and she replied within minutes: 'I was thinking about you last week!'

We met for coffee a month later. I was nervous. What if we had nothing in common any more? But after five minutes, we were laughing like ten-year-olds. She is a nurse now and has two children; I'm an engineer with none. Our lives are very different, but she is still the same generous, funny person.
Now we talk every Sunday. I've learned that real friendship doesn't disappear. Sometimes it's just waiting for someone to send a message.

listening.title: How Grandad met Grandma
listening.context: Saraa is interviewing her grandfather for a school project about family history.

lines.speaker: Saraa
lines.text: Grandad, can you tell me how you met Grandma?

lines.speaker: Grandad
lines.text: Of course. It was 1975. I was working as a bus driver in Ulaanbaatar.

lines.speaker: Saraa
lines.text: And was Grandma one of your passengers?

lines.speaker: Grandad
lines.text: Yes! She used to take my bus to the university every morning. She was studying medicine.

lines.speaker: Saraa
lines.text: So did you talk to her on the bus?

lines.speaker: Grandad
lines.text: Not at first. I was too shy. But one day, while she was getting off, she dropped her notebook. I ran after her with it.

lines.speaker: Saraa
lines.text: That's so romantic! What did she say?

lines.speaker: Grandad
lines.text: She said, 'Thank you. Now you have to buy me a cup of tea.' So I did. We got married a year later.

lines.speaker: Saraa
lines.text: Did you use to argue a lot?

lines.speaker: Grandad
lines.text: Hardly ever. She was always the sensible one, and I was the easy-going one. And this year is our fiftieth wedding anniversary.

writing.sample: I met my friend Ganbold when we were both working at a summer camp. We were very close, and we used to spend every weekend together: we used to go hiking, cook big dinners and talk until late. Then, three years ago, he got a job in Seoul. For a while we kept talking online, but one day, while we were planning his visit home, we had a silly argument about money and fell out. We didn't speak for a year. Last winter I bumped into his mother, and she told me that he missed me. I sent him a message and apologised. Now we video-call every month, and it feels like we never stopped being friends.
